item.title: What Does Their Belly Have to Do with Their Kidneys?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • New veterinary research reveals the gut and kidneys are in constant chemical conversation — and when that conversation breaks down, it actively drives chronic kidney disease forward in cats and dogs, not just marks its progression
  • Gut microbes produce over one hundred uremic toxins, with indoxyl sulfate and p-cresol sulfate the most studied; they build up as kidneys fail and worsen inflammation, muscle wasting, and kidney scarring
  • Cats as early as IRIS Stage 2 CKD already show elevated indoxyl sulfate levels, meaning this gut-driven damage begins long before most pet parents realize their cat’s kidneys are struggling
  • Targeting the gut has become a legitimate CKD treatment strategy — modified-protein diets, soluble fiber, prebiotics, carbon-based adsorbents, and essential amino acid support can reduce the toxin burden on failing kidneys
  • Constipation is a bigger deal than it looks: it keeps toxin-producing bacteria working longer and raises harmful uremic toxins in circulation, so treating it may help slow kidney disease progression

Most pet parents believe that the gut and the kidneys live in two separate mental compartments. The gut is where you worry about diet, diarrhea, and digestion, while the kidneys are connected to hydration, bloodwork, and, for a lot of senior cats especially, the slow drift into chronic kidney disease (CKD).

It turns out those compartments aren't really separate at all. The gut and the kidneys are in constant chemical conversation with each other, and when one side of that conversation goes sideways, the other one feels it.

The growing body of veterinary research now describes what's called the gut-kidney axis: the complex network of interactions between the gut microbiome, the lining of the intestines, the chemical byproducts of microbial digestion, and kidney physiology. The finding is that disruptions in this axis contribute meaningfully to the development and progression of CKD in cats and dogs, and that the gut itself is now considered a legitimate therapeutic target.

A Primer on the Gut-Kidney Connection

Your pet's gut hosts trillions of microorganisms: bacteria, fungi, and other microbes — that work alongside the body to digest food, synthesize nutrients, train the immune system, and maintain the gut lining. When that community is balanced, the system runs smoothly.

But when it's out of balance — a state called dysbiosis — harmful substances can leak into the bloodstream, forcing the kidneys to work harder to filter them out. Over time, this additional workload can contribute to kidney inflammation and damage.1

The relationship runs in both directions. As kidney function declines, waste products build up in the gut and shift the microbial community further out of balance, which creates more harmful byproducts, which puts more pressure on the kidneys. It's a loop — and once it starts turning, it's hard to break without targeted intervention.2

Uremic Toxins: The Specific Culprits

Researchers have identified over one hundred uremic toxins, which are waste products that accumulate in the blood as kidney function declines, and found that a sizable portion of them are generated by gut microbes. The most-studied in veterinary medicine is indoxyl sulfate (IS), with p-cresol sulfate (pCS) close behind. Both come from microbial breakdown of dietary protein in the colon.3

Normally, the kidneys clear these compounds out through urine. In pets with CKD, kidney filtration drops, so the toxins build up in circulation. And once they do, they cause real damage: they drive systemic inflammation, impair immune function, contribute to muscle wasting and weakness, injure the lining of blood vessels, and promote fibrosis — the scarring that progressively damages kidney tissue itself. In other words, these gut-derived toxins actively push CKD forward, not just mark its presence.4,5

Studies in cats have found that even those in the initial stages of CKD — IRIS Stage 2 — already have significantly higher indoxyl sulfate concentrations than healthy cats, meaning this imbalance begins early in the disease. In both cats and dogs, higher IS concentrations are associated with faster disease progression.6

What Dysbiosis Looks Like in a Pet with CKD

Cats with CKD have a measurably different gut microbiome than their healthy senior counterparts, with reduced microbial richness and shifts in the balance of bacterial species. Dogs with CKD show similar patterns, with higher relative abundance of some problematic bacterial genera (like Klebsiella and Clostridium) and lower abundance of beneficial ones (like Ruminococcus).

What drives these shifts? Several factors: the direct effect of urea breakdown raising the pH inside the colon, frequent use of antibiotics and phosphate binders in CKD pets, and dietary changes — especially reduced fiber intake. The leaky, inflamed gut lining that develops in CKD patients also lets more bacterial toxins slip into circulation, which perpetuates the whole cycle.7

Why This Changes the Treatment Conversation

For decades, veterinary CKD management has been largely symptomatic — controlling blood pressure, managing anemia, prescribing therapeutic diets, and addressing complications as they arise. The gut-kidney axis perspective looks at this from a different angle: if gut-derived toxins actively drive disease progression, then reducing those toxins becomes a direct way to slow the disease itself.

Several therapeutic strategies target this axis. None is a cure, but together they offer tools that didn't exist in the standard playbook a decade ago:8

  • Dietary management — Reducing dietary protein is already standard in CKD care, and the gut-kidney research helps explain why it works: Less protein in the colon means less raw material for microbes to convert into uremic toxins. Studies in both cats and dogs confirm that higher-protein diets lead to higher IS and pCS concentrations.

    For cats especially, who are obligate carnivores, the goal is a careful balance: enough high-quality, highly digestible protein to maintain lean body mass, but not so much that it feeds toxin production. Pairing modified protein with increased soluble fiber helps further by feeding beneficial bacteria and encouraging the production of helpful short-chain fatty acids.
  • Prebiotics and probiotics — Prebiotic soluble fibers feed beneficial bacteria and have been shown to reduce uremic toxin concentrations in CKD cats and dogs when added to a renal diet. Probiotic results have been more mixed in veterinary studies — one commercial probiotic (Enterococcus faecium SF68) didn't shift the microbiome or toxin levels in cats, while a different synbiotic product has shown contradictory results across studies. The honest state of the science: prebiotics look more consistently useful than probiotics in CKD pets right now, but research is ongoing.
  • Adsorbents — These are compounds that bind uremic toxin precursors in the intestinal tract so they can't be absorbed. A carbon-based adsorbent marketed for cats with kidney disease has been shown to reduce indoxyl sulfate levels in senior cats and cats with Stage 2 and 3 CKD after eight weeks of use.
  • Essential amino acids support CKD cats who commonly lose weight and muscle mass over time. A condition called protein-energy wasting has been found to worsen outcomes in CKD cats. Studies have found that fortifying renal diets with essential amino acids can help cats maintain lean body mass even while on protein-restricted food. The take-home: the quality of the protein matters at least as much as the quantity.

Don't Overlook Constipation

One of the more surprising pieces of the gut-kidney story is how much constipation matters. Cats with CKD tend to have less frequent bowel movements and are more likely to end up in the emergency room for constipation than healthy cats. The underlying mechanism makes sense: as the kidneys lose their ability to concentrate urine, the body compensates by reabsorbing water from the colon, which dries out the stool.

Constipation isn't just uncomfortable — it keeps fecal matter in the colon longer, giving microbes more time to convert amino acids into uremic toxin precursors. Human CKD patients with constipation have significantly higher serum concentrations of pCS and other toxins.

Treating constipation with hydration support, soluble fiber (like psyllium husk), osmotic stool softeners, and promotility agents may do more than just make your cat more comfortable — it may reduce the toxin burden their failing kidneys are trying to filter.9

What Pet Parents Can Watch For

Signs that your cat's gut or kidneys may be struggling — or that both systems are starting to pull each other down — include:10

  • Increased thirst or urination
  • Loss of appetite or fussy eating
  • Vomiting, especially in cats
  • Weight loss or visible muscle loss over the spine and hips
  • Lethargy or weakness
  • Changes in litter box habits — less frequent stools, straining, or very dry stools
  • A dull or unkempt coat
  • Breath that smells unusually strong (uremic breath)

None of these signs on their own confirm kidney or gut disease. But together, especially in a middle-aged or senior pet, they warrant a vet visit that includes bloodwork — not just a basic chemistry panel, but a full renal workup that includes SDMA (symmetric dimethylarginine), which can detect reduced kidney function earlier than creatinine alone and a urine sample.

Where That Leaves You

The gut-kidney axis isn't a wellness buzzword — it's a legitimate shift in how researchers are thinking about chronic kidney disease, and it's starting to shape how integrative and progressive vets manage it. The practical implications for pet parents are reasonable to act on now: feed a species-appropriate, highly digestible diet; include soluble fiber (through the diet itself or a vet-approved prebiotic); keep your pet well-hydrated; don't ignore constipation; and have an honest conversation with your vet about whether something like a carbon-based adsorbent or essential amino acid supplementation makes sense for your particular animal.

For senior cats especially — the population most likely to develop CKD — a yearly conversation about gut health alongside kidney bloodwork is a reasonable addition to the care plan. The two systems rise and fall together. Supporting both at once, rather than waiting for one to fail before paying attention to the other, is where the newest veterinary thinking is clearly pointing.

Your old friend's belly and their kidneys have more to say to each other than you might have realized. Learning to listen to both — and treating them as one connected system rather than two separate problems — is one of the more promising directions in senior pet care today.

  • 2,5,6 Royal Canin Academy, May 31, 2023

item.title: Highly Contagious Disease Still Threatens These Pets
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Canine distemper virus (CDV) is a highly contagious, life-threatening disease that is no longer common in the U.S., but still poses a threat to certain populations of puppies and dogs
  • Signs of distemper often follow a pattern that begins with upper respiratory tract symptoms and progresses to gastrointestinal symptoms, and finally to neurologic symptoms
  • Since there is no medical cure for canine distemper, treatment focuses on managing symptoms and making the patient as comfortable as possible using both conventional and alternative therapies
  • CDV can be prevented with a single well-timed vaccine, followed by a titer test four weeks post-vaccination to ensure immunity
  • Shelter and foster puppies, dogs from backyard breeders and imported dogs are most at risk, and the disease is fatal in about 50% to 75% of dogs with weak immune systems

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published April 24, 2019.

Because puppy shots include vaccination against distemper, fortunately, the virus — also known as Carre’s disease and once called “hard pad” disease — is relatively rare in dogs in the U.S. today.

Fortunately, not that long ago, the canine distemper virus (CDV) was a common killer of canine companions. Other animals, including cats, are also susceptible, but dogs are the primary host. The disease is caused by a type of Morbillivirus and is closely related to the measles virus in humans.

Despite the availability of distemper vaccines, cases of infection still occur occasionally, most commonly in shelter and foster puppies, dogs acquired from backyard breeders and dogs imported from outside the U.S. The rescued puppy population in shelters is at greatest risk for CDV due to a number of factors including stress, poor nutrition, immature or suppressed immune systems, the presence of gastrointestinal (GI) and/or external parasites, and other health issues.

How Canine Distemper Spreads

Non-immunized dogs who are exposed to an animal infected with CDV carry a high risk of contracting the disease, as do puppies born to an infected mother, and young dogs under extreme stress or who are immunocompromised. Dogs exposed to wildlife may also have a heightened risk of infection.

Bacterial infections, especially of the respiratory or GI tract, may also make dogs more susceptible to the virus. On rare occasions, improperly attenuated CDV vaccines have also been implicated as a cause.

Most dogs are exposed to the virus when they inhale the respiratory secretions of an infected animal, or come in direct contact with infected feces, urine or saliva. CDV can also be spread through direct or indirect contact with bedding, bowls or other items belonging to an infected dog.

In susceptible dogs (meaning dogs whose immune systems are unable to mount an effective defense), the virus first reproduces in the respiratory tract and then moves on to the lymph nodes and the lymph and blood circulatory systems throughout the body. CDV can also infect the skin, GI and urogenital tracts, central nervous system and other areas of the body.

Infected dogs can shed the virus for up to five days before symptoms appear, and for several months after exposure, even when no symptoms are present.

Symptoms of CDV

The period between exposure and the development of symptoms in unprotected dogs can be from about a week to as long as six weeks, however, most dogs become symptomatic within one to four weeks.

The virus often (but not always) follows a pattern in which symptoms first involve the upper respiratory tract, then the GI tract and finally the central nervous system. Initially, dogs show signs consistent with an upper respiratory infection, including a persistent cough, sneezing, discharge from the nose and eyes, a high fever (103.5 degrees F or higher), fatigue and lethargy.

At around the same time or just after the upper respiratory symptoms appear, as the infection moves to the GI tract, there can be vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite and weight loss.

Within one to three weeks, neurological signs may develop, including behavior changes, myoclonus (jerking muscles) and seizures — often a type called “gum chewing” in which the dog intermittently makes rhythmic chewing motions. Affected dogs are also susceptible to secondary bacterial infections.

The severity of symptoms varies depending on immune status. Dogs with competent immune systems are often able to successfully fight the infection, clear it from their bodies and suffer no long-term effects. Less fortunate dogs can end up with permanent tooth enamel, vision or neurologic damage.

In addition, certain strains of CDV can cause an abnormal enlargement or thickening of the pads of the feet, which is why the disease was sometimes called “hard pad” disease. In dogs with weak or compromised immune systems, death can result in two to five weeks after initial exposure, and sadly, this occurs about 50% to 75% of the time. Very young and elderly dogs have the highest rate of death from distemper.

Diagnosing Distemper

Veterinarians typically run a complete blood count (CBC) and serum biochemistry profile on dogs suspected of having contracted distemper. These tests provide a lot of information about the infection, organ function and the dog’s overall health.

A urinalysis is also performed, since viral antigens can be found in urine sediment. Advanced blood tests can reveal positive antibodies for the virus; however, these tests can’t distinguish between antibodies resulting from vaccination and those resulting from exposure to CDV. X-rays are really only necessary if pneumonia is suspected.

The best way to definitively diagnose canine distemper in a living dog is a fluorescent antibody test that can be performed on blood, respiratory or tonsil samples, cerebral spinal fluid, bone marrow or urine.

If the disease is in the very early stages, samples from the conjunctiva (the corners of the eye) can also be tested for antibodies. A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test is also now available that detects distemper virus in blood samples and is considered very reliable.

Ultimately, a distemper diagnosis can be confirmed by considering the dog’s history, the results of the veterinary exam and PCR testing with blood, urine or a conjunctival sample. On very rare occasions, there are cases of CDV that for whatever reason can’t be definitively diagnosed.

Treatment Options

No specific conventional therapy exists for canine distemper, so treatment focuses on managing symptoms and making the patient as comfortable as possible. The disease can be fatal, and the most important factor influencing a dog’s outcome is whether the virus has affected the central nervous system, and if so, to what extent.

Dogs diagnosed with CDV needs to be hospitalized and isolated from other animals. Conventional treatment includes antibiotics to address pneumonia if it’s present, cough medications, intravenous (IV) fluids, medications to reduce nausea and diarrhea, anti-seizure medications if necessary and pain management.

Integrative veterinarians will add intensive immune support during this time, including Kyosenex Prime (a purified thymus extract), IV vitamin C, hyperbaric oxygen therapy and ozone therapy as well. Many integrative/holistic veterinarians find homeopathic distemper nosodes very beneficial for reducing the duration of infection and minimizing the severity of symptoms and disease progression, especially if they’re used early on.

Since dogs can continue to shed the virus for weeks to months after recovery from distemper, they should be kept away from other dogs during this time. All surfaces, bedding and any object the sick dog has been in contact with should be cleaned and disinfected or thrown away. The virus is sensitive to ultraviolet light, heat and drying, and tends to linger in cold environments more so than in warm climates.

Preventing CDV

Veterinary vaccine authority Dr. Ronald Schultz believes one well-timed canine distemper vaccine for puppies is the best prevention against this highly contagious disease. Additional vaccinations against distemper are not necessary if a titer test completed two to four weeks after the vaccination shows the puppy was successfully immunized against the disease.

Dr. Richard Pitcairn, a homeopathic veterinarian and author of the bible of holistic health care for pets, “Dr. Pitcairn's Complete Guide to Natural Health for Dogs & Cats,” advocates the use of distemper nosodes prophylactically for puppies. In addition, creating a strong and vibrant immune system by making excellent nutritionally balanced, species-appropriate diet choices early on in a puppy’s life will help bolster your dog’s innate defenses against distemper and other infectious diseases.

The best way to definitively diagnose canine distemper in a living dog is a fluorescent antibody test that can be performed on blood, respiratory or tonsil samples, cerebral spinal fluid, bone marrow or urine.

If the disease is in the very early stages, samples from the conjunctiva (the corners of the eye) can also be tested for antibodies. A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test is also now available that detects distemper virus in blood samples and is considered very reliable.

Ultimately, a distemper diagnosis can be confirmed by considering the dog’s history, the results of the veterinary exam and PCR testing with blood, urine or a conjunctival sample. On very rare occasions, there are cases of CDV that for whatever reason can’t be definitively diagnosed.

Treatment Options

No specific conventional therapy exists for canine distemper, so treatment focuses on managing symptoms and making the patient as comfortable as possible. The disease can be fatal, and the most important factor influencing a dog’s outcome is whether the virus has affected the central nervous system, and if so, to what extent.

Dogs diagnosed with CDV needs to be hospitalized and isolated from other animals. Conventional treatment includes antibiotics to address pneumonia if it’s present, cough medications, intravenous (IV) fluids, medications to reduce nausea and diarrhea, anti-seizure medications if necessary and pain management.

Integrative veterinarians will add intensive immune support during this time, including Kyosenex Prime (a purified thymus extract), IV vitamin C, hyperbaric oxygen therapy and ozone therapy as well. Many integrative/holistic veterinarians find homeopathic distemper nosodes very beneficial for reducing the duration of infection and minimizing the severity of symptoms and disease progression, especially if they’re used early on.

Since dogs can continue to shed the virus for weeks to months after recovery from distemper, they should be kept away from other dogs during this time. All surfaces, bedding and any object the sick dog has been in contact with should be cleaned and disinfected or thrown away. The virus is sensitive to ultraviolet light, heat and drying, and tends to linger in cold environments more so than in warm climates.

Preventing CDV

Veterinary vaccine authority Dr. Ronald Schultz believes one well-timed canine distemper vaccine for puppies is the best prevention against this highly contagious disease. Additional vaccinations against distemper are not necessary if a titer test completed two to four weeks after the vaccination shows the puppy was successfully immunized against the disease.

Dr. Richard Pitcairn, a homeopathic veterinarian and author of the bible of holistic health care for pets, “Dr. Pitcairn's Complete Guide to Natural Health for Dogs & Cats,” advocates the use of distemper nosodes prophylactically for puppies. In addition, creating a strong and vibrant immune system by making excellent nutritionally balanced, species-appropriate diet choices early on in a puppy’s life will help bolster your dog’s innate defenses against distemper and other infectious diseases.

item.title: Your Best Friend Wants in on Your Self-Care Routine
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • A gentle Chinese bodywork technique called gua sha, the same scraping tool that’s taken over beauty routines, is quietly moving into integrative veterinary care, with some vets reporting better pain control in their patients
  • Using a smooth jade or rose quartz stone, practitioners glide along a dog’s neck, back, and limbs to boost circulation, release fascia, support lymphatic drainage, and trigger the body’s own endorphin response
  • Dogs most likely to benefit are those with muscle soreness, stiffness, arthritis, IVDD, slow surgical recovery, or age-related mobility issues — conditions where improved blood flow and fascia release can meaningfully ease discomfort
  • Studies suggest gua sha also helps proprioception, the body’s sense of where its limbs are in space, which can support dogs with neurological deficits or chronic pain who’ve become unsure of their footing
  • Gua sha is a complement to veterinary care, not a replacement, and should be learned from a vet trained in Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine before being done at home, especially on dogs with skin issues, tumors, or clotting disorders

You've probably seen the gua sha stones that have taken over the beauty world, those smooth, flat pieces of jade or rose quartz that people glide along their cheekbones and jawline in the morning for a de-puffed, glowing look. What you may not have seen is a growing group of integrative veterinarians using those same tools, with the same gentle scraping motion, on dogs. And they're reporting something worth paying attention to: better pain control, calmer behavior, and dogs who seem to melt into the sessions the way their humans do during a spa facial.

Gua sha for dogs sounds like one of those wellness trends that's about to collapse under its own silliness. It isn't. The technique is thousands of years old, and the mechanics that make it useful for human faces — moving fluid, releasing fascia, nudging circulation translate reasonably well to the muscles and connective tissue running along a dog's back and legs. Here's what it is, what it may do for your dog, and an honest look at the safety picture.

What Gua Sha Actually Is

Gua sha is a bodywork technique that goes back thousands of years in Traditional Chinese Medicine. The name roughly translates to "scraping sand." In practice, it means using a smooth-edged stone tool, typically jade, rose quartz, or a similar material, to make long, gentle strokes along the skin. The pressure moves stagnant fluid, boosts blood flow, and encourages the body's own healing responses. In TCM terms, it unblocks stuck Qi, or vital energy, that practitioners describe as the source of pain, inflammation, stiffness, and buildup of metabolic waste.1,2

The adaptation for dogs changes the pressure and the technique to suit a four-legged body, but the underlying idea is the same. The tool stretches and compresses the fascia, the thin connective tissue wrapping muscles, nerves, and organs, which prompts collagen cells to produce healthier tissue, reduces adhesions under the skin, and helps break up scar tissue from old injuries or surgeries.3

Why Some Vets Are Reaching for a Stone

Dr. Tori Counter of the Balanced Pet Vet, who introduced many pet parents to the practice, reports better pain control in her own patients since she started incorporating gua sha into their care. The scraping motion over a dog's neck, back, and limbs appears to reduce pain response and encourage the release of endorphins, the body's own feel-good chemicals. It's a similar reflex to the one that makes you rub your elbow after you bang it on a doorframe: gentle, rhythmic pressure signals the nervous system to turn the volume down on discomfort.4,5

A few studies also suggest the technique can help with proprioception, the body's sense of where its limbs are in space. That matters for dogs with intervertebral disc disease (IVDD), chronic pain, or neurological issues that leave them unsure of their footing. Gentle stimulation of the skin and underlying fascia seems to help the brain reconnect with those less-responsive areas.6

What It May Help With

Gua sha is a complementary therapy meaning it's meant to work alongside veterinary care, not replace it. The dogs most likely to benefit are those dealing with:7

  • Muscle soreness or stiffness from aging, over-exertion, or compensating for an injury
  • Recovery from injury or surgery, where circulation and lymphatic drainage support healing
  • Age-related mobility issues: stiff joints, slow mornings, that sense that getting up has become work
  • Chronic pain conditions like arthritis or IVDD, as part of a broader pain management plan
  • General stress, tension, or anxiety that lives in the body as tightness and bracing

It won't fix structural problems, cure disease, or replace what a veterinarian can diagnose and treat. It may make an older or hurting dog measurably more comfortable and give you a quiet daily ritual that supports whatever else they need.

The Tools Themselves

Gua sha tools are usually made from stone. Jade is a traditional choice associated with peace and good fortune. Rose quartz is linked to love and compassion. Some tools are also made from bian stone, bone, horn, and even stainless steel. For a dog, size and shape matter more than material. You want a smooth, rounded edge that glides along the body comfortably and fits well in your hand.8

Can You Do This at Home?

Here's where the two main schools of thought diverge, and it's worth hearing both.

Some integrative veterinarians, including Dr. Counter, teach clients to use gua sha at home. The appeal is practical: The cost is just the tool and some time learning the technique safely. Using it daily between professional sessions keeps movement flowing, speeds recovery, builds the bond between pet and parent, and costs far less than weekly acupuncture appointments. One guideline worth borrowing is to place your non-dominant hand over bony prominences like the spine, elbow, hips, or knees to protect them, so you're never scraping directly over bone.9

However, other veterinary experts urge caution about home use, pointing out that incorrect pressure or technique could cause bruising, discomfort, or injury. Their recommendation is to seek out a vet or certified canine rehabilitation therapist trained in Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine (TCVM) and let a professional handle it.10

For most pet parents, it’s best to start with a trained practitioner. Watch, ask questions, feel how much pressure is appropriate on your particular dog. Then, if your vet thinks it's safe, you can continue gentler maintenance sessions at home between appointments.

Where Not to Use It

Gua sha isn’t right for every dog or every situation, and their body usually tells you when something’s off. Avoid the technique on:11

  • Broken, irritated, or infected skin
  • Areas with tumors, lumps, or unexplained swelling
  • Dogs with blood clotting disorders or those on blood-thinning medication
  • Areas of acute injury or recent surgery not yet cleared by your vet
  • Any part of your dog's body where touch clearly makes them uncomfortable

If your dog pulls away, stiffens, or shows the stress signals you know in them lip licking, head turn, whale eye stop. The technique only works if the experience feels good.

How Often Should You Do It?

Frequency depends on the individual dog and what you're working with. A dog recovering from surgery may benefit from short, frequent sessions, while a senior dog with arthritis may do best with two or three focused sessions a week. A healthy adult may just enjoy a weekly session as part of a bonding ritual.

Consult with a qualified integrative veterinarian who can help you set a schedule that matches your dog's needs. However, keep in mind that not every groomer, massage therapist, or wellness practitioner is trained in gua sha and training matters.

Again, remember to look for a veterinarian or certified canine rehabilitation professional with specific credentials in TCVM or integrative therapies. Your regular vet can be a good starting point for a referral, and the American Holistic Veterinary Medical Association (AHVMA) keeps a directory of integrative practitioners.

The Takeaway for Pet Parents

Your dog doesn't need a 10-step wellness routine. But if you're already picking up gua sha stones for your own face in the morning, the idea of extending that quiet, deliberate care to the dog curled up at your feet isn't as fringe as it may sound. Done thoughtfully, with proper training, and in partnership with an integrative vet who knows your pet, gua sha can be a gentle, inexpensive addition to a holistic approach one that supports circulation, eases tension, and gives you a few quiet minutes together that have nothing to do with vet bills or medication schedules.

Some of the best things we can do for our aging dogs are the simplest. A warm hand. A smooth stone. A few minutes of attention. Your best friend was going to want in on your self-care routine eventually. Turns out they might have been onto something all along.

Sources and References

  • 1,7,10,11 Animal Wellness Magazine, September 28, 2026
  • 2,3,4,6,8,9 Balanced Pet Vet, Gua Sha for Dogs
  • 5 Resilience Integrative Veterinary Medicine, Dog Gua Sha

item.title: Freaks Out Your Dog, How to Ease the Distress
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Research out of Italy suggests petting a dog before leaving has a calming effect
  • The dogs in the study didn’t suffer separation anxiety; however, the results might indicate that advising owners to ignore these dogs as they prepare to leave is misguided
  • Because dogs with separation anxiety have no control over the genuine panic they feel, it stands to reason that gentle petting before departure has no power to reinforce behavior the dog isn’t choosing in the first place
  • Behavior modification, instituted as early as possible, is very important for dogs with separation anxiety
  • It’s also important to offer natural calming remedies to dogs living with the stress of separation anxiety

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published December 17, 2018.

Many owners with dogs who suffer from separation anxiety have been told by veterinarians, trainers and other knowledgeable people to ignore their pet for a short period before they leave the house, and also when they return. This approach is intended to make comings and goings a nonevent by ignoring the anxiety rather than reinforcing it by giving the dog attention. However, a study conducted by veterinary researchers in Italy seems to question this bit of conventional wisdom.

Pilot Study Looks at the Effect on Dogs of Gentle Petting Before Separation

The study involved a small group of 10 dogs without separation anxiety-related issues, and the goal was to determine whether gentle petting before the owner leaves for a brief period affects their dog’s behavior and physiology. The study was conducted at a neutral location for the dogs (a field). In the first experiment, the owners spent one minute petting the dogs before leaving them with a researcher. In the second experiment, the owners ignored their dogs for one minute before leaving.

In both experiments, the owners were absent for three minutes as they stood behind a shed where the dogs couldn’t see them. The researchers assumed the dogs also couldn’t pick up their owner’s scent behind the shed. The researcher left with the dogs simply stood in the field holding the leash until the owners returned after three minutes.

Results Show Petted Dogs Were Calmer and Less Stressed During Their Owner’s Absence

The dogs’ behavior, heart rate and salivary cortisol were measured both before and after their owner’s absence. The researchers observed that based on their behavior and low cortisol levels, the dogs weren’t highly stressed by the separation. However, in both experiments they spent about half the time (≈ 90 seconds) during the separation looking around for their owners.

In the first experiment in which the dogs were petted before their owners left, they spent more time showing calm behaviors during the separation, including lying down, sniffing the ground for three seconds or longer (versus sniffing for under three seconds, which can be a sign of stress). In addition, the dogs’ heart rates were lower after the first test than the second test in which they were ignored before the separation. The researchers concluded:

“This pilot study suggests that petting a dog before a brief separation from the owner may have a positive effect, making the dog calmer during the separation itself. Further studies are needed to analyze more in depth its effectiveness, especially in dogs affected by separation anxiety.”1

Very Important: Dogs with Separation Anxiety Aren’t ‘Acting Out’

It looks like we’ll have to wait awhile longer for additional research on how these study results apply to dogs with separation anxiety. Once dogs develop anxiety, this interaction may exacerbate their stress; that isn't yet known. The effect likely depends on the dog.

A soothing touch before leaving isn’t harmful in all cases, and might be beneficial to temporarily calm mildly stressed animals. As noted earlier, this approach is contrary to conventional wisdom on the subject, but it may turn out to be a case of “now that we know better, we can do better.”

Dogs with separation anxiety, most of whom grow anxious when they know their human is preparing to leave the house, are distressed and uncomfortable. They don’t choose to feel that way, so it doesn’t make sense that gently petting them before leaving would encourage them to choose to feel miserable the next time around. Said another way, dogs don't have the capacity to pretend to be anxious and upset when they’re not.

It’s likely unwise (and unkind) to view genuine anxiety and distress in dogs as a behavior they choose to perform — especially since we know canine separation anxiety is similar to panic attacks in humans, and is a condition over which they have no control. Common behaviors in a dog with separation anxiety include:

  • A need to be in the same room you're in, within a few feet of you
  • Frenzied greetings, whether you've been out of his sight five minutes or five hours
  • A noticeable mood change when he senses you're preparing to leave the house
  • Doing things while you're gone he doesn't do in your presence

When left at home alone, a dog with separation anxiety will often engage in at least one and often several of the following behaviors:

  • Vocalizing — This is typically barking, whining or howling that starts before you leave or soon after, and continues for most of the time you are away. Chances are your neighbors already have or will soon let you know there's a problem.
  • Drooling — Excessive salivation is considered by experts to be a red flag for separation anxiety when the excess drool only occurs when a dog is alone or believes she's alone.
  • Accidents in the house — Your dog has pee and/or poop accidents in random locations around your house rather than in one consistent spot, and this only happens when he's alone or believes he's alone.
  • Destructive behavior — Dogs with separation anxiety typically cause damage to doors or windows (exit points), or personal items such as clothing, pillows or the TV remote control. Confining these dogs to a kennel or carrier often causes an escalation of the behavior and can result in self-injury.

It’s very important to realize your dog's destructive, out-of-control behavior when he’s suffering a separation anxiety episode isn't intentional — it’s the result of the very real terror he's feeling.

Helping a Dog with Separation Anxiety

The goal in treating your dog’s separation anxiety is to reduce her dependence on you so that she can feel safe when you’re temporarily away from home. Helping her feel more self-sufficient can be accomplished with a variety of behavior modification techniques and other strategies.

What you absolutely never want to do is yell at or use physical punishment with your dog if you arrive home to destruction or a mess on the floor. It’s very important to remember that these are not signs of misbehavior, but clinical anxiety, and your dog isn’t in control when she’s doing them. Punishing her, especially after the fact, will only increase her anxiety level.

When you’re at home and going about your day or evening, train your dog to assume a calm, relaxed demeanor during “separations” when you’re in one room and she’s in another. First, move a short distance from her (while you’re in the same room) and then return and reward her with a treat.

Repeat this step at the same distance until you’re sure she’s very relaxed, and then gradually increase the distance until you’re almost out of the room, making sure to give praise and treats when she stays relaxed and in place. Once you’ve increased the distance until you’re out of your dog’s sight, you can begin to gradually increase the time she’s in one room and you’re in another. If the minute you’re out of sight your dog comes running, she needs more time to work up to that level of separation.

This can be a weeks- or months-long process, but it’s often very effective. If you don't feel your dog is making good progress or you feel you need guidance, it's recommended to talk with your veterinarian, a positive dog trainer or a specialist in canine behavior.

Additional Recommendations

Natural remedies are widely advocated to help minimize anxiety in dogs. Some suggestions:

  • Treat-release toys are a big hit with most dogs. There are chewing-type toys that can be filled with moist food. As he chews, the food is gradually released. You can even fill one up and put it in the freezer, which is especially useful for keeping a dog occupied for a longer period. There are also remote cameras and treat systems that let you talk to your pet while you’re at work or out of the house and dispense treats via an app.
  • Engage your dog in a rigorous exercise session daily. It can't be stressed enough how beneficial intense exercise is for anxiety. Also consider enrolling in a nose work class, which is a great way to help your dog build confidence. Go for a round of heavy exercise (or ball playing) before you leave. A tired dog gets into less mischief when left alone.
  • Invest in a pheromone diffuser, such as the Adaptil diffuser for dogs. Species-specific pheromones are chemical substances that can positively affect an animal's emotional state and behavior.
  • Consult a holistic or integrative veterinarian about homeopathic, traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) and Bach Flower Remedies that could be helpful in alleviating your pet's anxiety. Products commonly used, always in conjunction with behavior modification, include homeopathic aconitum or Hyland's Calms Forte, Bach Rescue Remedy, Solutions Separation Anxiety, Green Hope Farms Anxiety or other similar remedies depending on the animal.
  • Calming nutraceuticals and herbs that are often found most helpful include valerian and rhodiola, Again, you should consult your veterinarian about which option is right for your pet.
  • The essential oil of lavender has also been proven to reduce pets’ stress response. It's recommended to place a few drops on your dog’s collar or bedding before a stressor occurs, if possible, or diffuse the oil around your house for an overall calming effect.

If your dog's separation anxiety is severe enough that she’s very destructive when left alone or you're concerned she might hurt herself, you'll need to make other arrangements for her while you work to resolve her issues.

For example, consider taking her with you if possible. Alternatively, you can leave her with a caretaker — such as a friend who works from home or a retired neighbor or relative. Depending on your budget, you can also hire a dog sitter to stay in your home during your absence, or enroll her in doggy day care. With time, patience and persistence, most dogs with separation anxiety can be relieved of the worst of their troubling symptoms.

Sources and References

  • Psychology Today September 29, 2018
  • 1 Journal of Veterinary Behavior, September-October 2018, Volume 27, Pages 41-46

The researchers observed that based on their behavior and low cortisol levels, the dogs weren’t highly stressed by the separation. However, in both experiments they spent about half the time (≈ 90 seconds) during the separation looking around for their owners.

In the first experiment in which the dogs were petted before their owners left, they spent more time showing calm behaviors during the separation, including lying down, sniffing the ground for three seconds or longer (versus sniffing for under three seconds, which can be a sign of stress). In addition, the dogs’ heart rates were lower after the first test than the second test in which they were ignored before the separation. The researchers concluded:

“This pilot study suggests that petting a dog before a brief separation from the owner may have a positive effect, making the dog calmer during the separation itself. Further studies are needed to analyze more in depth its effectiveness, especially in dogs affected by separation anxiety.”1

Very Important: Dogs with Separation Anxiety Aren’t ‘Acting Out’

It looks like we’ll have to wait awhile longer for additional research on how these study results apply to dogs with separation anxiety. Once dogs develop anxiety, this interaction may exacerbate their stress; that isn't yet known. The effect likely depends on the dog.

A soothing touch before leaving isn’t harmful in all cases, and might be beneficial to temporarily calm mildly stressed animals. As noted earlier, this approach is contrary to conventional wisdom on the subject, but it may turn out to be a case of “now that we know better, we can do better.”

Dogs with separation anxiety, most of whom grow anxious when they know their human is preparing to leave the house, are distressed and uncomfortable. They don’t choose to feel that way, so it doesn’t make sense that gently petting them before leaving would encourage them to choose to feel miserable the next time around. Said another way, dogs don't have the capacity to pretend to be anxious and upset when they’re not.

It’s likely unwise (and unkind) to view genuine anxiety and distress in dogs as a behavior they choose to perform — especially since we know canine separation anxiety is similar to panic attacks in humans, and is a condition over which they have no control. Common behaviors in a dog with separation anxiety include:

  • A need to be in the same room you're in, within a few feet of you
  • Frenzied greetings, whether you've been out of his sight five minutes or five hours
  • A noticeable mood change when he senses you're preparing to leave the house
  • Doing things while you're gone he doesn't do in your presence

When left at home alone, a dog with separation anxiety will often engage in at least one and often several of the following behaviors:

  • Vocalizing — This is typically barking, whining or howling that starts before you leave or soon after, and continues for most of the time you are away. Chances are your neighbors already have or will soon let you know there's a problem.
  • Drooling — Excessive salivation is considered by experts to be a red flag for separation anxiety when the excess drool only occurs when a dog is alone or believes she's alone.
  • Accidents in the house — Your dog has pee and/or poop accidents in random locations around your house rather than in one consistent spot, and this only happens when he's alone or believes he's alone.
  • Destructive behavior — Dogs with separation anxiety typically cause damage to doors or windows (exit points), or personal items such as clothing, pillows or the TV remote control. Confining these dogs to a kennel or carrier often causes an escalation of the behavior and can result in self-injury.

It’s very important to realize your dog's destructive, out-of-control behavior when he’s suffering a separation anxiety episode isn't intentional — it’s the result of the very real terror he's feeling.

Helping a Dog with Separation Anxiety

The goal in treating your dog’s separation anxiety is to reduce her dependence on you so that she can feel safe when you’re temporarily away from home. Helping her feel more self-sufficient can be accomplished with a variety of behavior modification techniques and other strategies.

What you absolutely never want to do is yell at or use physical punishment with your dog if you arrive home to destruction or a mess on the floor. It’s very important to remember that these are not signs of misbehavior, but clinical anxiety, and your dog isn’t in control when she’s doing them. Punishing her, especially after the fact, will only increase her anxiety level.

When you’re at home and going about your day or evening, train your dog to assume a calm, relaxed demeanor during “separations” when you’re in one room and she’s in another. First, move a short distance from her (while you’re in the same room) and then return and reward her with a treat.

Repeat this step at the same distance until you’re sure she’s very relaxed, and then gradually increase the distance until you’re almost out of the room, making sure to give praise and treats when she stays relaxed and in place. Once you’ve increased the distance until you’re out of your dog’s sight, you can begin to gradually increase the time she’s in one room and you’re in another. If the minute you’re out of sight your dog comes running, she needs more time to work up to that level of separation.

This can be a weeks- or months-long process, but it’s often very effective. If you don't feel your dog is making good progress or you feel you need guidance, it's recommended to talk with your veterinarian, a positive dog trainer or a specialist in canine behavior.

Additional Recommendations

Natural remedies are widely advocated to help minimize anxiety in dogs. Some suggestions:

  • Treat-release toys are a big hit with most dogs. There are chewing-type toys that can be filled with moist food. As he chews, the food is gradually released. You can even fill one up and put it in the freezer, which is especially useful for keeping a dog occupied for a longer period. There are also remote cameras and treat systems that let you talk to your pet while you’re at work or out of the house and dispense treats via an app.
  • Engage your dog in a rigorous exercise session daily. It can't be stressed enough how beneficial intense exercise is for anxiety. Also consider enrolling in a nose work class, which is a great way to help your dog build confidence. Go for a round of heavy exercise (or ball playing) before you leave. A tired dog gets into less mischief when left alone.
  • Invest in a pheromone diffuser, such as the Adaptil diffuser for dogs. Species-specific pheromones are chemical substances that can positively affect an animal's emotional state and behavior.
  • Consult a holistic or integrative veterinarian about homeopathic, traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) and Bach Flower Remedies that could be helpful in alleviating your pet's anxiety. Products commonly used, always in conjunction with behavior modification, include homeopathic aconitum or Hyland's Calms Forte, Bach Rescue Remedy, Solutions Separation Anxiety, Green Hope Farms Anxiety or other similar remedies depending on the animal.
  • Calming nutraceuticals and herbs that are often found most helpful include valerian and rhodiola, Again, you should consult your veterinarian about which option is right for your pet.
  • The essential oil of lavender has also been proven to reduce pets’ stress response. It's recommended to place a few drops on your dog’s collar or bedding before a stressor occurs, if possible, or diffuse the oil around your house for an overall calming effect.

If your dog's separation anxiety is severe enough that she’s very destructive when left alone or you're concerned she might hurt herself, you'll need to make other arrangements for her while you work to resolve her issues.

For example, consider taking her with you if possible. Alternatively, you can leave her with a caretaker — such as a friend who works from home or a retired neighbor or relative. Depending on your budget, you can also hire a dog sitter to stay in your home during your absence, or enroll her in doggy day care. With time, patience and persistence, most dogs with separation anxiety can be relieved of the worst of their troubling symptoms.

item.title: Both Dogs and People Score a 'Win' When You Do This
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Researchers at Cornell University have completed the largest genetic study of dogs ever undertaken
  • There are over 350 diseases that affect both dogs and humans, and there are similarities in pathways and genes that cause those diseases
  • These study results will aid in the development of genetic tests for breeders to help create healthier populations of dogs
  • A citizen science project called Darwin’s Dogs is currently underway to gather data on how specific genes control the behavior and health of dogs
  • Nutrigenomics shows that what pets eat can suppress or unlock DNA, so a positive genetic marker doesn't mean a dog will automatically express every negative trait

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published June 29, 2016.

Not long ago, researchers at Cornell University wrapped up the largest genetic study of dogs ever undertaken by performing genetic mapping of 4,200 dogs, including purebreds, mixed breeds, and village dogs.1

The study examined 180,000 genetic markers that can help link specific inherited diseases with the genes responsible for them.

According to the Cornell Chronicle, the study is “ … [A] big step toward efficiently mapping genes responsible for complex diseases in dogs, most of which are very similar in humans, thereby accelerating our understanding of human genetic diseases.
By identifying important genes and proteins in dogs for diseases and traits, researchers may then test those homologous genes in humans.”2

Interestingly, there are over 350 diseases that affect both dogs and humans, and there are also similarities in the pathways and genes that cause those diseases.

The research team identified areas on the canine genome associated with hip and elbow dysplasia, idiopathic epilepsy (seizures with no known cause), lymphoma, mast cell tumors, and granulomatous colitis (Crohn’s disease).

Adam Boyko, Ph.D. of Cornell University’s College of Veterinary Medicine and lead author of the study believes the more we understand about the genetic basis of canine diseases, the more successful we can be in keeping purebred dog populations genetically healthy.

“Once you have these loci [DNA segments] identified, the future goal is to develop genetic tests so that breeders can test the dogs before they breed them and then make decisions to help create healthier populations,” says Jessica Hayward, Ph.D., a postdoctoral researcher at Cornell and study co-author.3

The good news for those of us with pets prone to genetic “breed flaws” is the emerging field of nutrigenomics that is proving that what we feed our pets has the power to suppress or unlock DNA.

This means even if your dog tests positive for genetic disease markers, it doesn’t mean he’ll automatically express all his negative genetic potential, which is comforting.

As owners, by positively modulating our pet’s environment — through excellent food choices, reducing chemical exposure and stressors, and focusing on physical fitness — we can dramatically reduce negative gene expression.

Are Genetics Also Shaping Your Dog’s Behavior?

According to Elinor K. Karlsson, Ph.D., an assistant professor at the University of Massachusetts Medical School (UMMS), a dog's personality is shaped by both his life experiences, and also thousands of years of evolution.

“Have you ever known a dog who would retrieve the same ball over and over again, for hours on end?” asks Karlsson, writing for the Conversation. “Or just wouldn’t stay out of the water? Or wasn’t interested in balls, or water, or but just wanted to follow her nose?”4

Karlsson believes these canine traits are the result of hundreds of generations of artificial selection by humans:

“By favoring useful behaviors when breeding dogs,” she says, “we made the genetic changes responsible more common in their gene pool.”5

Interested in Getting Involved in Doggy DNA Research?

To understand how specific genes control the behavior and health of dogs, much more information is needed. That’s why Karlsson and her colleagues have launched a citizen science research project called Darwin's Dogs.

For Darwin’s Dogs, Karlsson is asking dog guardians to record their own observations of their pet’s behavior and personality, and collect doggy DNA at home using mouth swabs provided by Darwin’s Dogs.

Karlsson and her team developed several short surveys to gather pet owner information about their dog’s diet, behavior, personality, and more.

The Darwin’s Dogs project is open to all dogs — purebreds and mixed breeds. The research team will use new DNA sequencing technology and analysis tools to collect genetic information from each dog. The goal is to conduct large-scale studies to facilitate rapid identification of important genes and genetic variants.

Karlsson plans to combine the genetic data from many dogs and look for changes in DNA that relate to particular behaviors. “It won’t be easy to match up DNA with an obsession with tennis balls, for instance,” says Karlsson. “Behavior is a complex trait that relies on many genes.”

Complex traits can be the result of tens or even hundreds of different genetic changes, and in addition, a dog’s environment plays a major role and adds to the complexity.

To be successful, Darwin’s Dogs needs lots of canine companions participating in the research project. Karlsson and her team hope to enroll 5,000 dogs initially. The more dogs they can involve, the more complex biological puzzles they can work to solve. According to Karlsson:

“This is a huge effort, but could offer huge rewards. By figuring out how a genetic change leads to a change in behavior, we can decipher neural pathways involved in psychiatric and neurological diseases shared between people and dogs. We already know these include not just anxiety, but also PTSD, OCD, autism spectrum disorders, phobias, narcolepsia, epilepsy, dementia and Alzheimer’s disease.”6

Karlsson and her colleagues are investigating both canine behaviors and diseases. Their theory is that by locating the genetic changes that led to complex behaviors (e.g., retrieving) and perhaps even personality characteristics, such as playfulness, they can learn more about how brains work. 

How to Participate in Darwin’s Dogs

The way the process works is that each participating dog guardian fills out a survey. After doing so, he or she will receive an easy-to-use kit to collect a small amount of their dog’s saliva to be used for DNA analysis. There’s no cost to the dog owner, and the researchers share any information they find. If you want to learn more and/or enroll your own dog in the Darwin’s Dogs citizen science research project, you can do so here.

Sources and References

  • 1 Nature Communications 7, Article Number 10460, January 22, 2016
  • 2 Cornell Chronicle, January 28, 2016
  • 3 The Cornell Daily Sun, March 8, 2016
  • 4,5,6 The Conversation, December 2, 2015

item.title: What if Their Behavior Problem Starts in Their Gut?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • New research on the microbiota-gut-brain axis shows your pet’s digestive system and brain are in constant two-way communication, meaning gut imbalances can directly fuel anxiety, aggression, and other behavior problems
  • Scientists have mapped four main communication routes between gut and brain: the vagus nerve, immune signaling, short-chain fatty acids from fiber fermentation, and neurotransmitters produced by gut microbes themselves
  • Studies in dogs and cats link disrupted gut microbiomes to anxiety, compulsive behaviors, and stress reactivity, with early trials showing that probiotics and dietary changes can measurably improve behavior
  • Gut-targeted interventions fall into four categories — probiotics, prebiotics, postbiotics, and synbiotics — each working through a different mechanism to restore the microbial balance behind calmer behavior
  • Before reaching for medication for a behavior problem, consider whether your pet’s gut health is contributing — a species-appropriate diet, targeted probiotics, and reduced environmental toxins often produce changes conventional training cannot

Your dog gets anxious every time you leave the house. Or they are reactive on walks. Or they bark at nothing for hours. Your cat sprays, hides, hisses when nobody has done anything wrong.

For decades, veterinary behavior medicine has treated problems like these as mental health issues — anxiety disorders, aggression, cognitive dysfunction — and reached for behavioral training, environmental changes, and sometimes psychotropic medications. All of that still matters. But a rapidly expanding body of research is pointing to something unexpected underneath many of these behavior problems: the gut.

A growing collection of peer-reviewed studies — in dogs, cats, humans, and rodent models — now suggests that the trillions of microbes living in your pet's digestive tract are actively influencing their mood, stress response, cognition, and behavior. The connection runs through what scientists call the microbiota-gut-brain axis, and it may be reshaping how we think about behavior problems in companion animals.

The Gut-Brain Axis in Plain Terms

The microbiota-gut-brain axis is a two-way communication network linking your pet's digestive tract to their central nervous system. It runs through four interconnected pathways: neural signals (primarily via the vagus nerve), endocrine signals (hormones), immune signals (cytokines and inflammatory messengers), and metabolic signals (molecules the gut bacteria themselves produce). Each pathway influences the others, and the whole system runs continuously in both directions.1

The gut microbiome is not a passive resident. It is an active mediator — producing neuroactive compounds including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), neurotransmitters, and vitamins that influence brain development, emotional regulation, and cognitive function. When the microbial community is in balance, this communication supports a steady, resilient nervous system. When it is thrown off — a state called dysbiosis — the signaling goes sideways, and behavior often follows.2,3

How Microbes Talk to the Brain

The science is still developing, but the main communication routes are now well-mapped. Researchers have identified several distinct pathways through which the gut microbiome exerts its influence on brain function and behavior, and these pathways do not work in isolation:

  • The vagus nerve — The longest cranial nerve in the body, running from the brainstem down through the chest and abdomen. Its sensory fibers in the gut wall detect microbial metabolites and transmit that information directly to the brain. Animal studies have shown that the behavioral effects of specific probiotic strains are abolished when the vagus nerve is cut — strong evidence that this nerve is a central pathway for gut-brain communication.4,5,6
  • Neurotransmitter production — Gut microbes directly produce or regulate neurotransmitters that affect mood, cognition, and behavior. Approximately 90% of the body's serotonin is synthesized in the gastrointestinal tract. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species produce GABA — the main inhibitory neurotransmitter involved in calming the nervous system — directly in the gut. Bacillus and Escherichia species produce dopamine precursors. Different microbial compositions produce different neurotransmitter profiles, which directly affects what your pet's brain has to work with.7
  • Short-chain fatty acids — When beneficial gut bacteria ferment dietary fiber, they produce SCFAs — including butyrate, propionate, and acetate — that cross the blood-brain barrier, reduce neuroinflammation, support the integrity of that barrier, modulate neurotransmitter synthesis, and regulate the body's main stress-response system (the HPA axis). SCFAs are among the most important chemical messengers in the whole axis.8
  • The HPA axis and stress response — The gut microbiota directly influences the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis — the body's central stress-response system. In germ-free animal studies, animals without gut bacteria show exaggerated stress responses and cognitive deficits. Introducing specific beneficial microbes normalizes those responses. In practical terms, this can mean that dysbiosis can keep a pet's stress system stuck in overdrive.9,10
  • Immune signaling and inflammation — Dysbiosis can compromise intestinal barrier integrity (sometimes called "leaky gut"), allowing bacterial components and inflammatory signals to enter the bloodstream. Those signals activate systemic immune responses, promote neuroinflammation, and can disrupt neurotransmitter metabolism — all of which affect behavior. Anxiety and depression in multiple species are consistently associated with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines.11

What Does This Mean for Dogs and Cats?

The research in companion animals is still catching up to the human and rodent work, but it is accelerating. Here is what has been established in dogs and cats so far:

  • Anxiety behaviors — In a group of 42 dogs classified by a veterinary behaviorist as aggressive, phobic, or healthy, aggressive dogs showed a significantly lower abundance of Bacteroidetes bacteria, along with changes in several other microbial genera. Phobic dogs showed an unexpectedly higher proportion of Lactobacillus — a reminder that the picture is nuanced.12,13
  • Aggression — A study of 31 American Pit Bull Terriers found aggressive dogs had a higher proportion of Firmicutes (particularly Lactobacillus) and lower levels of Proteobacteria and Fusobacteria. Non-aggressive dogs had higher levels of Bacteroides and Dorea strains.14
  • Separation anxiety — A 14-day supplementation study using Lactiplantibacillus plantarum PS128 in dogs with separation anxiety produced measurable stabilization of anxious behavior and changes in serotonin turnover — strong early evidence that specific probiotic strains can shift the behavior picture.15,16
  • Canine cognitive dysfunction — Older dogs show distinct gut microbiome patterns — lower proportions of Fusobacteria are associated with poor gut health and weight gain (and this finding is opposite that of aging humans), and lower levels of Actinobacteria are associated with improved cognition.17 Medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) supplementation has shown cognitive improvement in senior dogs, likely through microbial metabolism and ketone body production.18
  • Feline conditions — Research in cats lags behind dogs. However, bile acid dysmetabolism — specifically loss of the bacterium Peptacetobacter hiranonis — has been linked to feline neuroinflammation and cognitive dysfunction. Direct behavior-gut connections in cats remain preliminary, but they are increasingly on researchers' radar.19

Treatment Options That Target the Gut

Researchers reviewing this field group gut-targeted interventions into four main categories. Each one influences the gut-brain axis from a different angle. Here is how they break down:

  • Probiotics and psychobiotics — These are specific live bacterial strains administered for behavioral benefit. The best-studied in companion animals are Bifidobacterium longum BL999 and Lactiplantibacillus plantarum PS128, both of which have shown reductions in anxiety-related behaviors and stress hormone markers in canine trials. Not every probiotic strain does the same thing — strain specificity matters enormously, and most generic pet-store probiotics have no behavioral data behind them.20
  • Prebiotics — These are non-digestible fibers that feed beneficial bacteria. Fructo-oligosaccharides (FOS), galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS), and inulin promote the growth of SCFA-producing bacteria. Prebiotic trials have shown reduced waking cortisol and improved emotional bias in humans, and anxiolytic effects in rodents. Emerging evidence shows that combined prebiotic-probiotic (synbiotic) approaches may work better than either alone.21,22
  • Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) — This involves transferring microbial communities from healthy donors into dysbiotic recipients. It is still experimental in companion animal behavior medicine, but preliminary case reports in dogs with drug-resistant epilepsy and ADHD-like behaviors have shown improvement. FMT carries real risks — pathogen transmission, microbial disruption — and should be considered investigational, not routine.
  • Diet — It is the most modifiable factor shaping gut microbes. High-protein diets shift the microbial community toward protein-fermenting bacteria; high-fiber diets favor SCFA-producing species. Specialized diets like the ketogenic or MCT-enriched diet are showing growing evidence for cognitive dysfunction and epilepsy management in senior dogs. From the holistic integrative veterinary perspective, this is the single most practical lever most pet parents have.23

The Integrative Perspective

Integrative and holistic veterinarians have been raising the gut-behavior connection for years, and the mainstream research is now catching up. The practical takeaway from both camps looks remarkably similar: fresh, species-appropriate whole-food feeding supports a healthier microbiome; targeted probiotic and prebiotic use may support anxious or reactive pets as part of a broader plan; reducing environmental toxin load, chemical exposures, and chronic stress helps the microbiome do its job; and dietary interventions, when thoughtfully chosen, work with the body rather than against it.

From this perspective, a behavior problem may not just be a brain problem. It may be a whole-system imbalance — one that benefits from looking at diet, gut health, stress load, environmental enrichment, and the overall ecology your pet lives in. Behavioral training and conventional treatments still matter. But the research now suggests they will work better when the gut is pulling in the same direction.

What You Can Actually Do

Nothing in the emerging research replaces working with a veterinarian or veterinary behaviorist for serious behavior problems. But practical steps that support a healthier gut-brain axis, based on the current evidence:

  • Feed a fresh, whole-food, minimally processed diet with identifiable protein sources — this is the single biggest lever on microbiome composition
  • Include fiber from vegetables, fruits, and quality carbohydrate sources that feed SCFA-producing bacteria
  • Consider a quality probiotic matched to your pet's situation — ask an integrative vet about strain-specific choices with actual behavior data (like Bifidobacterium longum BL999 or Lactiplantibacillus plantarum PS128 for dogs with anxiety)
  • Add prebiotic foods or a prebiotic supplement, especially for pets with anxiety or digestive issues
  • Reduce ultra-processed kibble, which can promote dysbiosis over time
  • Avoid unnecessary antibiotics and medications where possible, since both can significantly disrupt the microbiome
  • Keep stress load manageable — predictable routines, adequate sleep, enrichment, calm handling
  • For senior pets showing cognitive changes, discuss MCT supplementation with an integrative veterinarian
  • Rule out underlying GI issues when a pet shows significant behavior changes — gut discomfort often shows up as behavior

What the Science Can and Cannot Say Yet

The researchers themselves are careful about overclaiming. Most of the current evidence base is correlative — showing that microbial differences and behavior differences coexist — rather than causal. Many studies have small sample sizes, variable methodology, and translate findings from rodents or humans to companion animals without direct canine or feline validation. The strain-specific effects of individual probiotics are still being mapped.

That said, the mechanistic science is solid, the direction of findings is consistent across species, and the practical interventions — diet, probiotics, prebiotics, reducing stress — carry low risk and growing benefit. The gut-brain axis is almost certainly going to be an increasingly important part of behavior medicine over the next decade. The pets whose humans start paying attention to this now are likely to benefit well before the field fully catches up.

Putting It All Together

The next time your pet exhibits a behavior problem that seems impossible to pin down, consider that the picture may extend beyond their brain. Trillions of microbes living in their gut are influencing their mood, their stress response, their cognition, and their day-to-day behavior through pathways science is still mapping. Supporting those microbes with thoughtful diet, strain-specific probiotics where appropriate, prebiotics, stress reduction, and an integrative approach to care may do more for your pet's behavior than any single intervention aimed at the brain alone.

Behavior starts somewhere. For a growing number of pets, that somewhere may be the gut. And that is genuinely good news — because unlike the brain, the gut is remarkably responsive to what you put into it every day.

Sources and References
